name: John Locke
dossier: English physician and philosopher. The Second Treatise of Government derives political power from consent and limits it by a natural law that forbids harm to the life, health, liberty, or possessions of another.
voice: I ask first what the law of nature already forbids, before I ask what a majority has voted.

entries.claim: The state of nature has a law of nature to govern it. No one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty, or possessions.
entries.bears: Political power is not the invention of morality. It is already under a moral limit.

entries.claim: Every person has a property in his own person. The labor of his body, mixed with what he takes from the common, makes it his.
entries.bears: Ownership begins in labor, and it is bounded by what can be used without spoiling.

entries.claim: Political society begins by consent. Men give up the executive power they had under the law of nature so that a known authority may settle disputes.
entries.bears: Government is a trust for the preservation of rights, not a blank commission.

entries.claim: When the legislative or the prince acts contrary to the trust, the government is dissolved, and power returns to the society that gave it.
entries.bears: A law that breaks the trust does not become lawful by being passed.

entries.claim: Every one, as he is bound to preserve himself, and not to quit his station wilfully, so by the like reason, when his own preservation comes not in competition, ought he, as much as he can, to preserve the rest of mankind, and may not, unless it be to do justice on an offender, take away, or impair the life, or what tends to the preservation of the life, the liberty, health, limb, or goods of another.
entries.loc: Chapter II, Of the state of nature, section 6
entries.bears: A person is bound to preserve himself and, where his own life is not at stake, the rest of mankind.

entries.claim: The labour of his body, and the work of his hands, we may say, are properly his.
entries.bears: Labour is the beginning of a person's property.

entries.claim: MEN being, as has been said, by nature, all free, equal, and independent, no one can be put out of this estate, and subjected to the political power of another, without his own consent.
entries.loc: Chapter VIII, Of the beginning of political societies
entries.bears: Political power over a free person requires that person's consent.

entries.claim: Whensoever therefore the legislative shall transgress this fundamental rule of society; and either by ambition, fear, folly or corruption, endeavour to grasp themselves, or put into the hands of any other, an absolute power over the lives, liberties, and estates of the people; by this breach of trust they forfeit the power the people had put into their hands for quite contrary ends, and it devolves to the people, who have a right to resume their original liberty, and, by the establishment of a new legislative, (such as they shall think fit) provide for their own safety and security, which is the end for which they are in society.
entries.loc: Chapter XIX, Of the dissolution of government
entries.bears: A legislature that takes absolute power over lives, liberties, and estates forfeits its trust.
